READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO CHAPTERS 5-7

  1. This sermon has been called
    1. "The Ordination Address to the Twelve" (Luke 6 parallel)
    2. "The Compendium of Christian Doctrine"
    3. "The Magna Carte of the KIngdom"
    4. "The Manifesto of the King"
      The title "Sermon on the Mount" was first coined by Augustine (A.D. 354-440) in his Latin Commentary on Matthew. This title came into our English Bibles through the Coverdale Bible of A.D.1535.

  2. This sermon has been called
    1. "The Ordination Address to the Twelve" (Luke 6 parallel)
    2. "The Compendium of Christian Doctrine"
    3. "The Magna Carta of the Kingdom"
    4. "The Manifesto of the King"

      The title "Sermon on the Mount" was first coined by Augustine (A.D. 354-430) in his Latin Commentary on Matthew. This title came into our English Bibles through the Coverdale Bible of A.D. 1535.

  3. "The Sermon on the Mount" in Matthew 5-7 is possibly the same as "the Sermon on the Plain" in Luke 6:17-49. The difference in the contents can be explained by comparing the target audiences of the Gospels writers.
    1. Matthew's readers were Palestinian Jews
    2. Luke's were Gentiles

       However, because the differences are so great, many believe they are not the same sermon. They may be examples of often repeated themes used by Jesus in many places with differing audiences. An example of this is the parable of the lost sheep. In Matthew 18 it was directed to disciples, but in Luke 15 to sinners.
       I have included my introductory notes from Luke 6 to highlight the difference between Matt. 5-7 and Luke 6:17-49.

       "There is an obvious difference between the "Sermon on the Mount," recorded in Matthew and the "Sermon on the Mount" in Luke (cf. Luke 6:17-49). Luke seems to be written on the level of social conditions and attitudes toward our material world (some scholars say Luke is dealing with a delayed Parousia; see Special Topic: A Delayed Second Coming); whereas Matthew seems to be written as a progression of spiritual levels progressing to Christlikeness (an eschatological setting; see Special Topic: The Second Coming).
       It is uncertain why Luke includes the "curses" (i.e. OT prophetic "woes." These woes are antithetically parallel to the blessings), while Matthew completely leaves them out (this shows the sermons recorded in the NT are not verbatim, but summaries and excerpts inspired by the Spirit; see Special Topic: Inspiration).
       Basically, the Beatitudes are not specific commands to be followed, but examples of an attitude toward our present world and our place in it. It is hard to decide whether or not Luke and Matthew record two different sermons using similar themes and examples. See

      1. Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, p. 312 and 366
      2. the same sermon recorded differently (see D. A. Carson, "Matthew" in Expositor's Bible Commentary)
      3. Remember, each of the Gospel writers selected, adapted, and rearranged Jesus' teachings to address their target audiences (see Fee, Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 12-148).
         Luke leaves out much of the Jewish elements in Jesus' teaching that Matthew records for his Jewish readership.
         Luke's version of Jesus' sermon has been greatly ignored by scholarship. Most interpreters use Matthew's account to interpret Luke's account. However, they are very different. Luke's beatitudes are not eschatological, but contemporary. Jesus is addressing His disciples (cf. Luke 6:20). The Kingdom is here (cf. Matt. 3:2; 4:17; 10:7; 12:28; Mark 1:15; Luke 10:9,11; 11:20; 17:21)! Believers' outward physical conditions must not affect their trust and joy in God."

  4. Under God's inspiration, the Gospel writers were free to select and adapt from Jesus' teachings and actions and to combine (i.e. arrange) them in non-chronological ways to communicate theological truth. See Fee and Stuart's How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth, pp. 127-148.
     The Gospels are not biographies—they are evangelistic tracts and discipleship manuals. Matthew combines Jesus' teachings and miracles into thematic units (5 major teaching events), while Luke records these same teachings in different contexts throughout his Gospel (i.e. Matt. 24 vs. Luke 17 and 21).

  5. The structure of Matthew's first and longest sermon by Jesus is very Jewish, possibly a conscious structural parallel to the Ten Commandments (i.e. Exod. 24:12). The statements are pointed gnomic sentences, often paradoxical (see Special Topic: Eastern Literature [biblical paradoxes), which attempt to summarize truth and aid memory. Thematically they are loosely related but grammatically separate.

  6. These teachings are the ultimate kingdom ethics meant to convict the lost and motivate the saved. The audience was comprised of several different groups (i.e. Matt. 5:25-26; Luke 6:18-19):
    1. the disciples Luke 6:20)
    2. the curious
    3. the sick
    4. the skeptical
    5. the religious elite looking for ways to attack Jesus

      Different texts were intended for the differing groups, but unfortunately, which one is never stated. However, the disciples are the primary audience, vv. 1-2.

  7. These teachings are basically an attitude toward life or a "worldview" which is radically reoriented toward faith and obedience to God (i.e. the New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34). There is an obvious play on Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 (see Special Topic: The Ten Commandments). The "Two Ways" of the OT (i.e. Deut. 30:15,19; Ps. 1) has been replaced by a grace first then Spirit-led Christlikeness. The goal is still a people who reflect YHWH's character, but the way has changed (i.e. human performance vs. divine mercy).

  8. The purpose is not to show the lost how to be saved, but how God expects the saved to live. The new kingdom ethic is so radical that even the most committed self-righteous legalists feel inadequate.
    1. grace is the only hope for salvation (i.e. Isa 55:1-3; Eph. 2:8-9)
    2. the Spirit's power the only hope for kingdom living (i.e. Isa. 55:6-7; Eph. 1:4; 2:10)

  9. I like what Dale Moody, "The Word of Truth," says: "The first part of each beatitude speaks of a condition in this present evil age, but the second part (of nine out of ten) speaks of the reward of the age to come," p. 527.
     I would add my thought to this quote: For believers the new age has already dawned. They can experience these "blessings" even now because we have a new mind, a new heart, a new spirit. For believers, the Kingdom is not only future (i.e. FUTURE TENSE in vv. 4-9), but present now (i.e. PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE vv. 3,10)!

  10. A good book which describes Jesus' teaching and preaching methods is Robert H. Stein's, The Methods and Message of Jesus' Teaching, Westminister Press, 1978, ISBN 0-664-24216-2.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO 5:3-12 (the BEATITUDES)

  1. In Matthew the Beatitudes form a spiritual ladder
    1. from salvation to Christlikeness
    2. from mankind's sense of spiritual need to mankind's new life in Christ.

      In the parallel (of Luke 6) the PRONOUN "you" is used referring to Jesus' disciples.

  2. Their number has been understood differently as either 7, 8, 9, or even 10.

  3. The Beatitudes (like parables) demand a response from the reader/hearer (as do parables)! They are not informational but motivational and transformational!

  4. Three helpful quotes:
    1. Every moral system is a road which by self-denial, discipline, and effort, men seek to reach the goal. Christ begins with this goal, and places His disciples at once in the position to which all other teachers point as the end. . .They began by commanding, He by bestowing: because He brings good tidings of forgiveness and mercy." The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah by Alfred Edersheim, p. 528-529.
    2. "The Sermon on the Mount is neither an impractical ideal nor a set of fixed legal regulations. It is, instead, a statement of the principles of life essential in a normal society. . .Many of the sayings of the Sermon are metaphorical or proverbial statements and are not to be understood in a literal or legal sense. In them, Jesus was illustrating principles in concrete terms." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. vol. 4 p. 2735.
    3. "Basic Principles:
      1. Character is the secret of happiness.
      2. Righteousness is grounded in the inner life. Character is not something imposed from without, but a life that unfolds from within.
      3. The inner life is a unity.
      4. Universal love is the fundamental social law.
      5. Character and life exist in and for fellowship with the Father. All worship and conduct look toward God.
      6. Fulfillment is the final test of life.
      7. Deeds and character are the only things that abide and endurance is the final test."
        The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. vol. 4 p. 2735.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Matthew 5:2 "began to teach them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2 "began to teach them" This is an IMPERFECT TENSE, which can mean

  1. He began to teach
  2. he continued to reiterate these things on different occasions

Matthew's Gospel is characterized by combining Jesus' teachings into topics. The content of Matthew 5-7 is scattered throughout Luke's Gospel.

entries.title: Matthew 5:3 "Blessed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:3 "Blessed" This term (Greek, makarios; Hebrew, ashere) meant "happy" or "honored" (cf. Matt. 5:3-11; "beautitudes" is the Latin word for "blessed"). The English word "happy" comes from the Old English "happenstance." Believers' God-given happiness is not based on physical circumstances, but inner joy.

There are no VERBS in these opening statements. They are EXCLAMATORY (cf. Rev. 1:3) in form like in Aramaic or Hebrew (cf. Ps.1:1). This blessedness is a current attitude toward God, a godly life, as well as an eschatological hope. A blessed person is the righteous person of Ps. 1:1-3; 119:1-2. This NT blessedness begins with faith in Jesus (i.e. Eph. 2:8-9) and must result in godly living (i.e. Eph. 2:10)!

▣ "poor in spirit," Two terms in Greek were used to describe poverty (this is how Luke used the term in Luke 6:20); the one used here was the more severe of the two. It was often used of a beggar who was dependent on a provider. In the OT this implied hope in God alone (the parable of Lazarus and the rich man, i.e. Luke 16:19-31)! Matthew makes it clear that this does not refer to physical poverty (i.e. Luke 6:20), but to spiritual inadequacy. Man must recognize God's adequacy and his own inadequacy (cf. John. 15:5; 2 Cor. 12:9). This is the first truth of the gospel message (i.e. human need, cf. Rom. 1:18-3:31). Possibly these first few beatitudes reflect Isa. 61:1-3 (quoted by Jesus in Luke 4:18-19), which predicted the Messianic blessings of the coming New Age.

Special Topic: The Gospel

▣ "kingdom of heaven" This phrase, "Kingdom of Heaven" (Matthew only) or "Kingdom of God" (Mark and Luke) is used over 100 times in the Gospels. In the Luke 6:20 parallel, it is the "kingdom of God." Matthew was writing for people with a Jewish background who were nervous pronouncing God's name because of Exod. 20:7. But the Gospels of Mark and Luke were written to Gentiles. The two phrases are synonymous (i.e. Matt. 19:23-24 vs. Mark 10:23,25). The phrase refers to the reign of God in human hearts now (i.e. Matt. 4:17) that will one day be consummated over all the earth (cf. Matt. 6:10; 16:28; 26:29). This is possibly confirmed by Matthew alternating between PRESENT TENSE "is" in Matt. 5:3b and 10b, and FUTURE TENSE "shall be" in the second phrase of Matt. 5:4-9 (i.e. current reality but future hope).

Special Topic: The Kingdom of God

entries.title: Matthew 5:4 "mourn"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:4 "mourn" This referred to "loud wailing" (penthos, cf. Matt. 9:15), which was the strongest term for mourning in the Greek language. The context implies that the mourning was for our sin. The result of seeing one's sin (Matt. 5:3) must be repentance.

It is possible, if the OT referent is Isa. 61:1-3, that it was mourning in a corporate, societal sense.

Special Topic: Repentance (NT)

▣ "comforted" This concept is used often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 12:1; 40:1; 49:13; 51:3,12; 52:9; 66:13). The new age has dawned in Christ. God comforts not only the OT people of God (i.e. forgives, accepts, and cares for) but all who believe/trust Jesus (i.e. Eph. 2:11-3:13). The OT promises to Israel have been universalized to the whole world (cf. John 1:29; 3:16; 4:42; 12:47; 1 John 2:2; 4:14).

Special Topic: Comfort

Special Topic: Faith, Believe, or Trust

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Matthew 5:5 "gentle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5 "gentle" This is literally "meek" or "humble." Moses is called by the term in the OT (i.e. Num. 12:3). Jesus used this term for Himself (cf. Matt. 11:29; also note the OT quote from Zech. 9:9 in Matt. 21:5). Its origin implies domesticated strength, like a trained mule, camel, or horse. Recognizing our need for God and His provision in Christ makes believers humble and teachable (cf. Eph. 4:2; 1 Pet. 3:4).

▣ "inherit the earth" This phrase was often associated with the Promised Land (cf. LXX of Ps. 37:11), but it could be an eschatological reference for the entire earth (cf. Isa. 11:6-9). This reflects the ambiguity of the Hebrew term erets (BDB 75), here, the Greek term "gē." Again, God's OT promises to Israel have been universalized to all mankind.

It is not by power but by Spirit that evil is defeated (note Zech. 4:6). The earth was created for a place of fellowship between God and His highest creation.

Special Topic: Believers' Inheritance

Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth

Special Topic: World (several terms), II. D.

entries.title: Matthew 5:6 "hunger and thirst"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:6 "hunger and thirst" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE describing the basic ongoing spiritual needs of humankind (cf. John. 4:10-15). This imagery reflects a kingdom person's ongoing attitude toward God (cf. Ps. 42:1-4; 63:1-5; 84:1-4; Isa. 55:1-5,6-12). This is a sign that the image of God, lost in the fall, has been restored through Christ.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NET  "for righteousness"
TEV  "to do what God requires"
NJB  "for uprightness"
REB  "to see right prevail"
Peshitta  "for justice"

This key theological term can mean

  1. a declared (legal) or imputed (banking) right standing (cf. Rom. 4)
  2. a personal kingdom ethic, Matthew uses the term for Jewish ritual righteousness in Matt. 6:1
  3. Special Topic: Almsgiving

It involves both justification and justice; both sanctification and sanctified living! This is another example of Matthew's CIRCUMLOCUTION, a substitution of another word or phrase for the name of God (cf. Matt. 5:7-8).

"Rightouesness," here is another CIRCUMLOCUTION for "God."

Special Topic: Righteousness

▣ "satisfied" Literally "gorged," this term was used of fattening cattle for market.

entries.title: Matthew 5:7 "merciful"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7 "merciful" Mercy is the result, not the grounds, of knowing God. It is the ability to put one's self in another's situation and act with compassion (cf. Luke 6:35-38).

A change occurs here in the beatitudes. The two previous ones have focused on the Kingdom person's sense of spiritual need; the following ones, however, focus on the attitudes that motivate one's actions. This was what was missing in Pharisaism then and legalism now.

▣ "they shall receive mercy" This is a FUTURE PASSIVE INDICATIVE which is literally translated "shall be mercied." The implications of this tense are:

  1. the FUTURE TENSE was used in the sense of certainty now, in this age
  2. the future forgiveness in the Last Day Judgment (eschatology) scene

The PASSIVE VOICE may be another CIRCUMLOCUTION like "kingdom of heaven," to avoid using God's name.

The shocking opposite of a forgiving spirit is an unforgiving person (i.e. Matt. 6:14-15; 18:35; Mark 11:25 (v. 26 is a textual addition, see Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, p. 110). Also note the shocking parallel in James 2:13, as well as Luke 6:37-38!

Special Topic: Greek Verb Tenses Used for Salvation

entries.title: Matthew 5:8 "pure in heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:8 "pure in heart" Our attitudes are crucial (cf. Titus 1:15; Heb. 12:14). Priorities are equally crucial. From Ps. 24:4; 51:10; and 73:1, "pure" can mean

  1. single-minded
  2. focused
  3. cleansed

This term was used in the OT (LXX) for ritual washings. Notice the focus is on the heart, the center of the individual's being, not the intellect or ritual actions. The central aspect of personhood in the OT was the "heart," while in Greek thought it was the "mind" (i.e. Mark 12:29-30)

Special Topic: The Heart

▣ "shall see God" "See," probably in the sense of fully knowing Him and understanding His ways! To the pure in heart, God can be seen in all creation and in every situation. Purity opens the spiritual eyes.

In the OT to see God meant to die (cf. Gen. 16:13; 32:30; Exod. 3:6; 33:20; Jdgs. 6:22, 23; 13:22; 1 Kgs. 19:13; Isa. 6:5; see note on Exod. 24:11 online). This statement, therefore, would probably refer to both a current reality (i.e. see God in other Christians, cf. Heb. 12:14) or an eschatological setting.

Special Topic: Can Humans See God and Live?

entries.title: Matthew 5:9 "peacemakers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:9 "peacemakers" This compound word appears only here. It refers to reconciliation between God and humanity (i.e. the gospel of Jesus Christ), which results in peace between persons. However, this is not a peace at any price, but peace through repentance and faith (cf. Mark 1:15; Acts 3:16,19; 20:21; Rom. 5:1). God has not changed, humanity has (i.e. Genesis 3; Rom. 3:9-19; Gal. 3:22), but in Christ the original mindset has been restored.

Once we have peace with God restored by the gospel, we can help others find the same peace. God's original purpose in creation was fellowship with His human creation. True peace can be found only in relationship with our Creator. His stated and recurrent "will" is that all come into fellowship with Him.

Special Topic: Peace (NT)

Special Topic: Peace and War

▣ "sons of God" In the OT this phrase usually referred to angels (see first Special Topic below). It is a Hebrew idiom reflecting God's character (see second Special Topic below). The goal of Christianity is Christlikeness (cf. Rom. 8:28-29; 1 Cor. 3:18; 7:1; Gal. 4:19; Eph. 1:4; 4:13; 1 Thess. 3:13; 4:3,7; 5:23; 1 Pet. 1:15), which is the restoration of the image of God in mankind lost in the Fall of Genesis 3 (see third Special Topic below).

Special Topic: Sons of God in Genesis 6

Special Topic: "sons of. . ." (OT)

Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind

entries.title: Matthew 5:10 "those who have been persecuted"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10 "those who have been persecuted" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE. It speaks to those who have been and continue to be persecuted by an outside agent (i.e. Satan, demonic, unbelievers). The persecution of believers is a real possibility, even an expected reality, for God's children in a fallen world (cf. Matt. 5:11-12; Acts 14:22; Rom. 5:3-4; 8:17; Phil. 1:29; 1 Thess. 3:3; 2 Tim. 3:12; James 1:2-4; 1 Pet.3:14; 4:12-19; Rev. 11:7; 13:7). Notice the suffering is occurring because of the godly lifestyle and witness of believers. God uses it to make believers like Christ (cf. Rom. 8:28-30; Heb. 5:8).

This verse is a needed balance to the modern American (health, wealth and prosperity, see Gordon Fee, The Disease of the Health Wealth Gospel) overemphasis on the covenant promises of Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29 applied directly and unconditionally (i.e. ignoring the curses for disobedience) to all believers. Health, wealth, and prosperity promises must be balanced by the repeated acknowledgment of the suffering of believers, because they are people of faith in a fallen, godless world. Jesus suffered, the Apostles suffered (i.e. example, Paul, 2 Cor. 4:7-12; 6:3-10; 11:23-30), the early Christians suffered, so shall believers in every age!

Special Topic: Why Do Christians Suffer?

entries.title: Matthew 5:11 "insult you and persecute you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:11 "insult you and persecute you" These are both AORIST SUBJUNCTIVES which denoted a contingency but with a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL structure which showed it was potential (cf. Rom. 5:3-5; James 1:2-4; 1 Pet. 4:12-19). Persecution may be common, but it is not to be desired or pursued (as did many of the early church fathers). In the OT, problems and persecution were often interpreted as a sign of God's displeasure because of sin (cf. Job, Psalm 73, and Habakkuk deal with the subject). The righteous do suffer. But Jesus went one step further. Those who live and witness for Him will suffer rejection and persecution from a fallen world as He did (cf. John. 15:20; Acts 14:22; 2 Tim. 3:12).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "and falsely say all kinds of evil against
  you"
TEV  "and tell all kinds of lies against you"
NJB  "and speak all kinds of calumny against
  you"

There is some manuscript doubt about the PRESENT PARTICIPLE "falsely." It is missing in the western uncial manuscript D, the Diatesseron, and the Greek texts used by Origen, Tertullian, and Eusebius. It is included in the early Greek uncial manuscripts א, B, C, W, and the Vulgate and Coptic translations. The UBS4 gives the inclusion of "falsely" a "C" rating (difficulty in deciding). The UBS3 had given it a "D" rating.

It does reflect the historical situation of the early church. The early Christians were accused of incest, cannibalism, treason, and atheism. All of these accusations were related to misunderstandings about Christian terms and worship practices (cf. 1 Pet. 2:12,15; 3:16).

▣ "because of Me" This is linked to Matt. 5:10. The persecution discussed is specifically related to being an active follower of Christ (cf. 1 Pet. 4:12-16).

entries.title: Matthew 5:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:11-12 A new paragraph should start with Matt. 5:11 (cf. NRSV & TEV). The syntactical structure of the Beatitudes changes from vv. 3-10. Luke 6:22-23 has an even stronger wording.

entries.title: Matthew 5:12 "Rejoice and be glad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:12 "Rejoice and be glad" These are two PRESENT IMPERTIVES (cf. Acts 5:41; 16:25). Rejoicing comes from being counted worthy to suffer for/with Christ and being rewarded (cf. Acts 5:41; Rom. 8:17; 1 Pet. 4:14,16). Be careful of self pity. Nothing "just happens" to God's children (cf. Rom. 5:2-5; James 1:2-4, see Hannah Whithall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life). Suffering has a purpose in the plan of God.

Special Topic: Why Do Christians Suffer?

▣ "for your reward in heaven is great" See Special Topic: Degrees of Rewards and Punishment.

▣ "the prophets" This was a veiled reference to Christ's Deity. As the prophets of the OT suffered because of their relationship with and service to YHWH, so too, the Christian will suffer because of his relationship with and service to Christ.

entries.title: Matthew 5:13 "You are the salt of the earth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:13 "You are the salt of the earth" Because of the extreme value of salt in the ancient world

  1. for healing and cleansing
  2. for preserving food
  3. for flavoring food
  4. for sustaining moisture in humans in very dry climates
  5. for fertilization for crops

Salt was a prized possession. It was often used to pay soldiers' wages. Christians are called the "salt of the earth" because of their penetrating and preserving power in a lost world.

"You" is PLURAL and emphatic, like Matt. 5:14. Believers are salt (cf. Mark 9:50). It is not an option. The only choice is what kind of salt will they be. Salt can become adulterated and useless (cf. Luke 14:34-35). Lost people are watching.

Special Topic: Salt

▣ "if salt has become tasteless" This is a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE which meant potential action. Literally salt cannot lose its strength but when mixed with impurities the salt can leach away and, thereby, the salt content is diluted. Christians can lose and/or damage their testimonies!

The term "tasteless" was normally used in the sense of "foolish" (cf. Rom. 1:27; 1 Cor. 1:20).

▣ "It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled under foot by men" Salt that was unusable as a preservative or flavor enhancer was absolutely useless. It was thrown on the footpaths or roof tops to form a hard top seal. Salt taken from the Dead Sea had many impurities. The people in this part of the world were accustomed to unusable salt.

In this context, this imagery applies to those who heard Jesus speak but did not act on His teachings.

entries.title: Matthew 5:14 "You are the light of the world"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:14 "You are the light of the world" Light has always been biblical imagery for

  1. revelation (1 Pet. 2:9)
  2. truth (John 1:9; 1 John 2:8)
  3. salvation (Ps. 27:1; John 1:4-5)
  4. guidance (Ps. 119:105)
  5. moral purity (1 John 1:7)

It was used by Jesus to describe Himself (cf. John. 9:5). The question is not, "Will you be the light of the world?" As a believer, you are the light of the world (cf. Phil. 2:15). The only real question is, "What kind of light will you be?" All that some people know about God, they know from you and your life! "You" is PLURAL and emphatic like Matt. 5:13.

Special Topic: Light

5:15
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta, NET  "a basket"
NKJV  "the bushel basket"
TEV  "a bowl"
NJB  "a tub"
REB  "a meal-tub"

This referred to an earthen pot used for measuring grain.

▣ "lampstand" There was a small protrusion from the wall in ancient Palestinian homes on which a small oil lamp was placed which gave light to the whole room (cf. Mark 4:21-22; Luke 8:16-17).

entries.title: Matthew 5:16 "Let your light shine. . .
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:16 "Let your light shine. . . This is an AORIST IMPERATIVE. Believers' lifestyles must bring glory and honor to God (i.e. "sons of God" in Matt. 5:9, cf. Eph. 1:4; 2:8-10). It is possible that the thrust of this verse related to the exclusivism and cloistering of groups like the Essenes. Believers must stay engaged with an evil society, but not become part of it (cf. John. 17:15-18).

▣ "Father" The normal posture for Jewish prayer was standing with the eyes open and the head and arms lifted upward. They prayed as if in dialogue with God.

Jesus' use of the title Father to describe YHWH is one of the unique aspects of His teachings. Matthew records Jesus' use of the title for God over forty times.

Special Topic: Father

Special Topic: The Fatherhood of God

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. To whom are these statements directed?
  2. Can anyone meet these standards?
  3. Why do Matthew and Luke record the same sermon differently?
  4. Why are these statements so paradoxical?
  5. How do the Beatitudes relate to each other?
  6. What is the purpose of the Sermon on the Mount?
  7. Write the central truth of each paragraph in your own words and then summarize the whole.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO MATTHEW 5:17-48

  1. Jesus has just set out the New Covenant ethic (i.e. vv. 1-16). How is it related to the OT? To understand Matt. 5:17-20 one must realize that Jesus is rejecting the Jewish oral tradition (Talmud) which attempted to interpret the written Old Testament. Jesus elevated the inspired and eternal OT in His strong and definitive statements (i.e. Matt. 5:17-19), then showed Himself to be its true fulfillment and ultimate interpreter (i.e. 5:21-48). This can be seen in the fact that Jesus used the phrase "you have heard" not "it is written." This is a powerful Christological passage, in light of the Jews' respect for the written and oral Law.

  2. Jesus not only claimed authority over rabbinical interpretation (i.e. v. 20), He even corrects Moses in vv. 31-32!!
     There are several Mosaic Laws that Jesus addressed.
    1. the one in Matt. 5:31-32
    2. the sabbath ultimacy in Mark 2:23-28
    3. the food laws in Mark 7:19
    4. deemphasizes the temple in John 4:19-26
    5. "the Law and the Prophets" only lasted until John the Baptist, Matt. 11:12-13; Luke 16:16; Ronm. 3:19-31
    6. challenged the High Priest in Matt. 26:63-654
    7. also note the Church Council of Acts 15:6-21

      It is impossible to follow the Mosaic Covenant without a temple and a priesthood. A.D. 70 removed these cultic necessities!
      Special Topic: Paul's Views of the Mosaic Laws
      Special Topic: The Superiority of the New Covenant Over the Mosaic Covenant
      Special Topic: Jesus Is Greater Than

  3. This section is not exhaustive of the misinterpretations of first century Judaism but representative. The entire sermon, Matthew 5-7, is an attitude check for humble believers and a pride killer for self-righteous legalists (Jewish and Christian). Jesus placed the mind alongside the hand as the source of sin and rebellion against God's law. He addressed the inner man as well as the outer. Sin begins in the thought life.

  4. God's standard of judgment is so different from fallen mankinds (cf. Isa. 55:8-9). Believers' righteousness is both an initial gift and a developing Christlikeness, both a forensic, legal position and a Spirit directed progressive sanctification. This section focused on the latter.
    Special Topic: Sanctification

  5. The two best intepretations of the purpose of the Mosaic Covenant are:
    1. Galatians 3
    2. the book of Hebrews

      Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from OT Covenant Promsies?

  6. If these verses were spoken in the historical context of modern conservative Christianity, we would all be shocked at how God views our religiosity!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Matthew 5:17 "Do not think"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:17 "Do not think" This is a NEGATIVE AORIST ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE which was a grammatical construction that meant "do not ever start!"

▣ "that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets" What does "abolish" mean? It is used in several contexts.

  1. Matt. 5:17 ‒
    NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB  "abolish"
    NKJV  "destroy"
    TEV  "to do away with"
    Peshitta  "weaken"
  2. Matt. 24:2 ‒ destroy the temple
  3. Matt. 26:61 ‒ also destroy the temple
  4. note usage in Acts 5:38-39, where it refers to Gamaliel's quote, "it will be overthrown"
  5. Possibly it refers to ending the OT sacrificial system as a way for sinful humans to approach a holy God. The new way is the once and for all sacrifice of Jesus. This is Paul's summary of Rom. 1:15-3:20 in the powerful words of Rom. 3:21-31.
    Special Topic: Paul's Views of the Mosaic Law
    Special Topic: The Superiority of the New Covenant Over the Mosaic Covenant

The context of Matt. 5:17-20 is a statement affirming the inspiration and eternality of the Old Covenant. Jesus acted in a sense as the second Moses, the new Law-giver. Jesus Himself was the fulfillment of the Old Covenant. The New Covenant is a person, not a set of required rules. The two covenants are radically different, not in purpose but in the means of accomplishing that purpose (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). The thrust here is not on the inability of the Old Covenant to make man right with God as in Galatians 3, but rather on the rabbis' incomplete and improper interpretation of the biblical texts by means of their Socratic or dialectical method of interpretation.

Jesus, in effect, expanded the scope of the Law from overt actions to mental thoughts. This takes the difficulty of true righteousness through the Old Covenant to a level of utter impossibility (cf. Gal. 3:10,21-22). This impossibility will be met by Christ Himself and given back to the repentant/believing faith community through imputed righteousness or justification by grace through faith (cf. Rom. 4:6; 10:4; 2 Cor. 5:21). Mankind's religious life is a result of a relationship with God, not a means to that relationship.

▣ "the Law or the Prophets" This was an idiom referring to two of the three divisions of the Hebrew Canon: Law, Prophets and Writings (see Special Topic: Hebrew Canon. It was a way of designating the entire Old Testament. It also showed that Jesus' understanding of Scripture was closer to the theology of the Pharisees than of the Sadducees, who only accepted the Torah, or Law (Genesis – Deuteronomy) as authoritative.

It must be remembered that the OT prophets were covenant enforcers. They spoke to the covenant people about the blessings of obedience and the curses of disobedience! They did not have a new message, apart from the Torah (Gen. ‒ Deut.). The New Covenant in Jesus makes the first covenant irrelevant (i.e. Heb. 8:13).

Special Topic: Pharisees

Special Topic: Sadducees

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "but to fulfill"
TEV  "but to make their teachings come
  true"
NJB, REB  "to complete"

The word used here is used (twice) to denote that which is "completed," consummated," "fulfilled." Note the SYNONYMS.

  1. "until all is accomplished" ‒ Matt. 5:18
  2. to establish the law ‒ Rom. 3:31
  3. the goal or end of the law ‒ Rom. 10:4

The New Covenant (Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36) has fulfilled the purpose/goal of the Mosaic Covenant in bringing sinful humans into fellowship with God.

Special Topic: Paul's Views of the Mosaic Law

entries.title: Matthew 5:18 "truly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:18 "truly" This is literally "Amen." See Special Topic: Amen

▣ "heaven and earth" In the OT these two permanent entities were used as the two required witnesses to confirm YHWH's statements (cf. Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:15). They are aspects of our world that will remain as long as this age remains. This statement was like an oath from YHWH.

Special Topic: Heaven

▣
NASB  "not the smallest letter or stroke"
NKJV  "one jot or one tittle"
NRSV, NET  "not one letter, not one stroke of a letter"
TEV, REB  "not a letter, not a dot"
NJB  "not one dot, not one little stroke"
Peshitta  "not even a yod or a dash"

This referred to

  1. the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet, yod, paralleled in the smallest letter in Greek alphabet, iota
  2. the ornamental additions to squared Hebrew script, similar to serifs in modern calligraphy
  3. a small stroke that distinguishes between two similar Hebrew letters (i.e. ד [d] and ר [r])

The point is that the OT is significant in all its parts; even its most seemingly insignificant parts were from God. Yet the OT was completely fulfilled in the person, work, and teachings of Christ.

▣
NASB  "shall pass from the Law until all is
  accomplished"
NKJV, Peshitta  "will by no means pass. . .till all is
  fulfilled"
NRSV  "will pass. . .until all is accomplished"
TEV  "will not be done away with—until the
  end of all things"
NJB  "is to disappear. . .until all its purpose
  is achieved"
REB  "will disappear from the Law until all that
  must happen has happened"

The first term usually referred to destroying something by pulling it down, like a wall. The second term was used in Matt. 1:22 to fulfill, as in accomplishing its declared function. Although this term had several other meanings in other parts of the NT, here it speaks of the OT finding its completion in Christ. Jesus' teachings are like the new wine that cannot be contained in the old wine skins (cf. Matt. 9:16-17).

This fulfillment referred to Jesus' life, death, resurrection, second coming, judgment, and eternal reign, which are, in some sense, incipient in the Old Testament. The OT points to Christ and His work. The Apostles interpreted the OT in a typological or Christological sense! The NT is about Jesus, not Israel!

entries.title: Matthew 5:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:19 This verse is not a threat directed toward modern interpreters and teachers, but a rejection of Pharisaic traditional legalism, spiritual arrogance, and sectarian dogmatism. Jesus Himself clearly set aside the Oral Tradition (Talmud), but also parts of the written Law! See list in Contextual Insights, B.

▣ "least. . .greatest" The use of "least" and "greatest" may be evidence for some type of gradation within the Kingdom (cf. Matt. 20:20-28; Luke 12:47-48; 1 Cor. 3:10-15).

Special Topic: Degrees of Rewards and Punishment

Special Topic: Rabbinical Hermeneutics

entries.title: Matthew 5:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:20 This was/is a shocking statement to sincere, legalistic religionists. Self-righteousness is a common plague of religious mankind (cf. Isa. 29:13; Col. 2:16-23). Neither correct doctrine (James 2:19) nor religious actions (Matt. 7:21-23) replace the need for a personal repentance/faith relationship (cf. Mark 1:15; Acts 3:16,19; 20:21; Phil. 3:8-9; Rom. 10:3-4).

Matthew 5:20 and 48, are keys to interpreting the whole Sermon on the Mount.

Special Topic: Pharisees

Special Topic: Scribes

▣
NASB, Peshitta  "will not"
NKJV  "by no means"
NRSV, NJB, REB  "will never"

This is the doubling of two Greek terms for negation. One functions with the INDICATIVE MOOD and the second with the other Greek MOODS. It was a very emphatic grammatical way to negate a statement (cf. Matt. 5:18,26; 10:23,42; 13:14; 15:6; 16:22,28; 18:3; 23:39; 24:2,21,34,35; 25:9; 26:29,35).

Special Topic: Greek Grammatical Terms, VIII

▣ "the kingdom of heaven" Special Topic: The Kingdom of God

entries.title: Matthew 5:21 "You have heard that the ancients were told"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:21 "You have heard that the ancients were told" This could be understood as "to the ancients" (i.e. recipients) or "by the ancients" (i.e. originators). The first part of this verse is from the Ten Commandments.

The second part is harder to identify and may be a quote from the rabbinical schools (Shammai, the conservative, or Hillel, the liberal) referring to local synagogue courts. The Greek text has "judgment" not "court." This implied a rejection of Pharisaic scribal interpretation, while at the same time asserting the inspiration of the OT.

Special Topic: The Ten Commandments

▣ "murder" This is a quote from the Septuagint (LXX) of Exod. 20:13 or Deut. 5:12. It is a FUTURE ACTIVE INDICATIVE used as an IMPERTATIVE.

  1. The KJV translates this as "kill," but this rendering is too broad in scope.
  2. The NKJV has "murder."
  3. A more accurate translation would be "nonlegal premeditated murder." In the OT there was a legal premeditated murder―the "Blood Avenger" (cf. Deut. 19; Num. 35; Josh. 20).

Special Topic: Murder (Exod. 20:13)

Special Topic: Blood Avenger

▣ "to the court" See full note at 5:22 for options.

entries.title: Matthew 5:21-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:21-26 This paragraph deals with New Covenant believers' attitudes and actions toward covenant brothers and sisters (i.e. the new redeemed community). True Christianity is relational and corporate!

Special Topic: Biblical Faith is Corporate

entries.title: Matthew 5:22 "But I say to you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:22 "But I say to you" Jesus' teaching was radically different from the rabbis of His day, whose authority was found in quoting previous Jewish teachers as their authority (cf. Matt. 7:28-29; Mark 1:22; Luke 4:32). His teachings amazed the Jewish crowds (cf. Matt. 13:54; 22:33; Mark 6:2; 11:18). Jesus' authority lay in Himself. He is the true revealer of the true meaning and implications of the Old Testament. Jesus is Lord of Scripture. The "I" is emphatic―"I myself and no other" or "myself (as the Son of God who knows the mind of God.)"

Special Topic: Jesus and the Mosaic Law

Special Topic: Jesus Is Greater Than

▣ "everyone who is angry" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE PARTICIPLE. This was the Greek term for a settled, nurtured, non-forgiving, long term anger (orgē). This person continued to be intensely angry.

▣ "with his brother" The KJV adds "without cause." This is a Greek manuscript variation. The addition is not in the early Greek manuscripts P67, א* (Sinaiticus), B (Vaticanus), or the Vulgate. However, it is in the uncial manuscripts אc, D, K, L, W, the Diatesseron, and the early Syrian and Coptic translations. The UBS4 gives the shorter text a B rating (almost certain). The addition weakens the strong thrust of the passage.

It might be helpful at this point to explain the superscripts:

  1. the * means the oldest copy of the manuscript type that is available
  2. the c means the later correctors of copyists. This is often represented by 1, 2, 3, etc, if there is a series of correctors
  3. the number after P refers to the papyrus manuscript
  4. uncial Greek manuscripts are designated by capital letters, while papyrus manuscripts are designated by numbers

Special Topic: Textual Criticism

▣
NASB, TEV, REB  "good-for-nothing"
NKJV, Peshitta  "Raca"
NRSV, TEV  "insult"
NJB  "fool"

Raca was Aramaic for "an empty-headed person incapable of life." This section is not dealing with what specific titles one can or cannot call another person, but with a supposed believer's attitude toward others, especially covenant brothers.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB. NET  "fool"
TEV  "a worthless fool"
NJB  "traitor"
Peshitta  "you are effeminate"

The Greek term, mōros, translated "fool," was meant to reflect the Aramaic term raca. However, Jesus' word play was not to the Greek word mōros, but the primarily Hebrew word mōreh, BDB 598, which meant "rebel against God" (cf. Num. 20:10; Deut. 21:18,20; see F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, p. 42). Jesus called the Pharisees by this very term in Matt. 23:17.

Not only our actions, but our motives, attitudes, and purposes determine sin against our fellow human. Murder, as far as God is concerned, can be a thought! Hatred of our brother or sister clearly shows that we do not know God (cf. 1 John. 2:9-11; 3:15, and 4:20, or lack of forgiveness, cf. Matt. 6:14-15; 18:21-35). Socially speaking, a hateful thought is better than a death, but remember that this section of Scripture is meant to shatter all self-righteousness and pride in one's own goodness. It is possible that this threefold expression was a sarcastic play on scribal interpretation methods.

Special Topic: Terms for Foolish People

▣
NASB  "the supreme court"
NKJV, NRSV  "the council"
TEV  "the Council"
NJB  "the Sanhedrin"
REB  "the court"
Peshitta  "before the congregation"

As is obvious from the translations, there are two possibilities.

  1. the Sanhedrin (DEFINITE ARTICLE)
  2. a local synagogue court (v. 25)

I think #2 fits the context best. It seems unlikely a minor issue such as this would come before the major judicial body of the nation of Israel. The Greek text simply has "the council." The NASB has "court" in vv. 21,22, but it is literally the Greek word "judgment" with the DEFINITE ARTICLE.

Special Topic: Sanhedrin

NASB, NET  "fiery hell"
NKJV, NJB, Peshitta, REB  "hell fire"
NRSV  "the hell of fire"
TEV  "fire of hell"

This is a transliteration to the Hebrew term Gehenna (i.e. "the valley of the sons of Hinnom"), which refers to the garbage dumb of Jerusalem. Jesus and Jesus alone (except for one time in James 3:6) uses the term Gehenna, which speaks of eternal punishment. See
Special Topic: Where Are the Dead?, II. D., and V.

Recently I have become aware of two YouTube videos about the early church's views on Hell. I recommend them to you.

  1. Edward Fudge, "The Fire That Consumes"  YouTube One Hour Lecture
  2. Steve Gregg, "Hell ‒ Three Christian Views"  YouTube Lecture - 1:34:57

Special Topic: Eternal Punishment (Hell)

entries.title: Matthew 5:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:23 This is a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which means probable action.

Special Topic: Greek Grammatical Terms, VII.

▣ "presenting your offering at the altar" This strongly implies that Matthew wrote before the destruction of the temple by the Roman general Titus in A.D. 70. There is a new academic book that suggests that all the books of the NT were written before the destruction of the temple (i.e. Redating the New Testament, by John A. T. Robinson).

Lifestyle love precedes religious acts! Relationships take precedence over ritual (note Micah 6:6-8). People are the top priority with God.

Notice that the person who feels wronged is "your brother" (twice), not the one presenting the offering. Disruptions in interpressonal relationships affect acts of worship! On my! Believers are their brothers' "keeper"! See Special Topic: Christian Freedom and Christian Responsibility

Jesus illustrates how the second greatest commandment, "love your neighbor as yourself" (Lev. 19:18), really works out in life and worship!

entries.title: Matthew 5:24 "be reconciled to your brother"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:24 "be reconciled to your brother" This is an AORIST PASSIVE IMPERATIVE. Personal relationships are more significant than

  1. periodic ritual (Matt. 5:24)
  2. judicial decisions (Matt. 5:25)

The VERB "be reconciled" is a compound of the PREPOSITION dia, meaning "by means of" and allassō, meanng "to change" or "to exchange." It is used only here. Normally in the NT, the PREPOSITION is kata, meaning "throughout" or possibly "completely" (cf. Rom. 5:10; 1 Cor. 7:11; 2 Cor. 5:18-20).

This is my exegetical note from 2 Cor. 5:18, 19, 20.

2 Cor. 5:18 "reconciled" This is a major theological truth. The word basically means to exchange or change and thereby to bring together that which was alienated. Rebellious humans have been brought back into fellowship with God through Christ. God exchanged Christ's righteousness (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21) for their sin. Christ died in our place (cf. Isa. 53 [quoted in Acts 8:32-33]; Mark 10:45; Rom. 5:12-21; 2 Cor. 5:14,21).

This context (i.e. 2 Cor. 5:16-21) and Rom. 5:10-11 are the definitive passages on this theological term. Sinners are now friends, even family, with the Holy One. Restoration of the fellowship damaged in the Fall (cf. Genesis 3) has been made complete in Christ.

A discussion of "reconciliation" as a theological concept is in Frank Stagg's New Testament Theology, pp. 102-104, 142.

▣ "and gave us the ministry of reconciliation" Theologically this is parallel to 2 Cor. 5:14-5. Jesus became believers' reconciliation, now they must become the means of sharing the gospel of reconciliation with others. Believers share in Jesus' death (cf. Rom. 6:3-11) and we share in His ministry (cf. 2 Cor. 5:19). Christlike service is the goal (cf. 1 John 3:16).

5:19 "He has committed to us the word of reconciliation" A lost world is not on the doorstep of a powerless, loveless God, but is on the doorstep of an apathetic, unconcerned church.

  1. we have the message
  2. we have the keys of the Kingdom (cf. Matt. 16:19; Rev. 1:18; 3:7)
  3. we have the indwelling Holy Spirit (cf. Rom. 8:9,11; 1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19; 2 Tim. 1:14)
  4. we have the marching orders of Jesus (cf. Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:46-47; Acts 1:8)

What will we do?

5:20 "be reconciled to God" This is a PRESENT PASSIVE IMPERATIVE. Is this a command to lost people or to saved people? The larger context is mandating an appropriate lifestyle on the part of believers. Jesus saved us from sin and strife; we are saved to serve! We are called to Christlike ministry, not personal agendas.

This context has a message to a lost, needy world-Christ died for you (positional righteousness). This context has a message for a factious, unloving church-Christ died for you (progressive righteousness).

The PASSIVE VOICE could be translated

  1. "let God reconcile you to Himself"
  2. "allow yourselves to be reconciled" (cf. The Jerome Biblical Commentary, p. 281)
  3. "let God change you from enemies into his friends" (cf. TEV)

Believers proclaim the truth, the Spirit convicts the lost, the Son provides the means, and the Father accomplishes His will through covenant response.

entries.title: Matthew 5:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:25 In this context Jesus is talking about a legal case between two Jews before a Jewish judge (or synagogue court). In 1 Corinthians 6 Paul discusses a legal lawsuit between another citizen (maybe a believer, maybe not) before a pagan judge. See my full exegetical notes online.

entries.title: Matthew 5:26 "Truly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:26 "Truly" See Special Topic: Amen.

▣ "until you have paid the last cent" "Cent" is the smallest Roman coin, quadrans. Judgment extracts the full penalty. Mercy and love forgive all (note Jesus' parable in Matt. 18:21-35)!

Special Topic: Coins Used in Palestine in Jesus' Day

entries.title: Matthew 5:27 "adultery"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:27 "adultery" Here the term is moichaomai. It is a quote from the Ten Commandments found in Exod. 20:14 and Deut. 5:18.

  1. In th LXX if is porneia, which usually referred to extramarital intercourse, but it also had the added connotation of any improper extramarital sexual activity, such as homosexuality or bestiality.
  2. In the OT adultery was a sexual affair involving a married person. Jesus redefined sexual sin as an attitude of the heart.

Sex is a gift of God, a good and wholesome thing. But God has also put boundaries on its expression for our well-being and long term enjoyment. Prideful, self-centered humans always want to go beyond the God-given bounds. These words of Jesus by inference would also refer to premarital sexual activity.

Special Topic: Adultery (Exod. 20:14)

Special Topic: Human Sexuality

entries.title: Matthew 5:28 "heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:28 "heart" See Special Topic: Heart.

entries.title: Matthew 5:29, 30 "If"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:29, 30 "If" These are FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCES which were assumed to be true from the author's perspective or for his literary purposes. Humans have been affected by Genesis 3. We are not what we were created to be.

Special Topic: Greek Grammar, VI.

Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind

▣
NASB, Peshitta  "makes you stumble"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV  "causes you to sin"
NJB, REB  "should be your downfall"

This term was used of the baited, triggering mechanism of an animal trap. See the parallel in Mark 9:43-48 and Jesus' second mention of this subject in Matt. 18:8-9. Since all humans are affected by sin (different ones for different individuals), we must take personal responsibility to remove ourselves from places/things/occasions of temptation (i.e. Proverbs 1-9; Eph. 4:27; 6:10-18; James 4:7; 1 Pet. 5:8-9). We will not be able to blame Satan, or heredity, or circumstances for our sins when we all stand before God and give an account of the gift of life (cf. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15). We are free moral agents made in God's image, accountable to Him for our lives!

The footnote in George M. Lamsa's translation of the Peshitta into English, p. 955, states that "cut it off" is an Aramaic idiom for "stop stealing."

▣ "lose" This term (apollumi; AORIST MIDDLE SUBJUNCTIVE is in both Matt. 5:29 and 30. It denotes "perishing" or "destroying" (cf. John 3:16; NASB 1970)

Special Topic: Destruction (apollumi)

entries.title: Matthew 5:29, 30 "hell"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:29, 30 "hell" There is eschatological divine punishment (i.e. Gehenna) and sin is the ticket to get in! See my note at Matt. 5:22.

Special Topic: Where Are the Dead?, II. D. and V.

Special Topic: Eternal Punishment

entries.title: Matthew 5:29, 30 "hell"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:29, 30 "hell" There is eschatological divine punishment (i.e. Gehenna) and sin is the ticket to get in! See my note at Matt. 5:22.

Special Topic: Where Are the Dead?, II. D. and V.

Special Topic: Eternal Punishment

entries.title: Matthew 5:29-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:29-30 This is obviously hyperbolic for emotional impact! It is not meant to be taken literally! Sin is dangerous and its consequences eternal! See Robert Stein, The Method and Message of Jesus' Teaching.

Special Topic: Judgment in the NT

entries.title: Matthew 5:31 "sends his wife away"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:31 "sends his wife away" Matthew 5:27-32 and 19:3-12 deal with the same issue (i.e. human sexuality). Be careful not to read your preconceived cultural notions into these passages! In context, Jesus was showing the ways that one commits adultery other than those taught by the Scribes:

  1. mental lust
  2. putting away one's spouse except for sexual unfaithfulness (cf. Deut. 24:1)

Jesus shows Himself to be Scripture's proper interpreter by changing a decree of Moses (also see my notes at. 5:17-19).

Special Topic: Human Sexuality

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB  "a certificate of divorce"
TEV  "notice of divorce"
NJB  "a writ of dismissal"
Peshitta  "divorce-papers"
NET  "a legal document"

This is a quote from Deut. 24:1-4. Moses did this to protect the wife who had no rights or resources at all in that day and culture. Remarriage was assumed. However, Jesus asserted in addressing His disciples that was a concession to their fallenness, not God's ideal. Remember, all of the Sermon on the Mount is addressing the New Covenant disciple. Divorce is not the unpardonable sin (see my exegetical notes on 1 Cor. 7), but it is a failure which affects societal stability. For other understandings of Deut. 24:1-4, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 175-176; also note the discussion of Mal. 2:16 on pp. 349-351.

Special Topic: Certificate of Divorce

5:32
NASB, NRSV  "except for the reason of unchastity"
NKJV  "for any reason except sexual immorality"
TEV  "she has not been unfaithful"
NJB  "except for the cause of an illicit marriage"
Peshitta  "except for fornication"

This "exception clause" is unique to Matthew's Gospel (i.e. 5:32; 19:9). Probably because it related to Jewish views of inheritance rights given by YHWH which Gentiles would not comprehend.

"Unchastity" is the term porneia. This referred to any kind of sexual misconduct. This was often interpreted as "fornication" or "unfaithfulness." There were two rabbinical schools of interpretation developed in the second temple period:

  1. Shammai, who allowed divorce for inappropriate sexual activity only ("some indecency," Deut. 24:1)
  2. Hillel, who allowed divorce for any reason (i.e. "she finds no favor in his eyes," Deut. 24:1)

Divorce had become a problem within Judaism. Some scholars see this term related not to sexual intercourse, but to incest (cf. Leviticus 18; 1 Cor. 5:1) or even the ability to have children (i.e. menstrual period). Still others think it relates to the issue of virginity discussed in Deut. 22:13-21. In the OT adultery and/or conception affected family inheritance, which was sacred and given by YHWH (Joshua 12-24). The "Year of Jubilee" is an illustration of this concern.

Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.

▣
NASB, NET  "makes her commit adultery"
NKJV, Peshitta  "causes her to commit adultery"
TEV  "he is guilty of making her commit adultery"
NJB  "makes her an adulteress"
REB  "he involves her in adultery"

This is an AORIST PASSIVE INFINITIVE. The PASSIVE VOICE is crucial in a proper interpretation of "causes her to commit adultery" (the Markan parallel, 10:11,12, is the VERBAL form that can be PASSIVE or MIDDLE VOICE). The very act of divorcing a wife caused the woman to be stigmatized by the community as an adulteress whether or not she was guilty. The one remarrying her also became stigmatized. This is not a dogmatic statement referring to remarriage as being adultery.

  1. A. T. Robertson in his Word Pictures in the New Testament, vol. 1 p. 155).
  2. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 43,54-55

It needs to be stated that this difficult subject of divorce must be dealt with in context (see Fee, Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 131-133. Here, it is a message to disciples, while in Matt. 19:1-9, Mark 10:2-12. and Luke 16:18, the setting is Pharisaic trick questions. We must guard against forming our theology on divorce by merging these contexts and claiming to have Jesus' neutral theological views on the subject.

For my exegesis of the NT texts on divorce, see my notes online and audio tapes #2130 and 2131, in the second green box on my home page, www.freebiblecommentary.org

Special Topic: Greek Grammatical Terms, II

entries.title: Matthew 5:33 "vows"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:33 "vows" This was an allusion to several OT texts (i.e. Lev. 19:12; Num. 30:2; Deut. 23:21). This did not mean cursing, but God's name being brought into a conversation to assure the truth of one's statements (i.e. "swears," cf. Matt. 23:16-22; James 5:12). Vows or oaths in the OT could refer to

  1. worship (cf. Deut. 6:13; see Special Topic: Worship)
  2. legal proceedings (cf. Exod. 20:7; Lev. 19:12)
  3. affirmations of doing something (cf. Leviticus 27; Num. 30:2; Deut. 23:21-22)

The focus is not on oath taking, but on failing to perform the vow!

  1. Jesus was involved in an oath in Matt. 26:63-64.
  2. Paul made oaths in 2 Cor. 1:23, Gal. 1:20, Phil. 1:8, and 1 Thess. 2:5.
  3. Another oath is found in Heb. 6:16.

entries.title: Matthew 5:34 "make no oath"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:34 "make no oath" Jesus testified under oath in Matt. 26:63-64. Paul often confirmed his words by oaths in God's name (cf. 2 Cor. 1:23; Gal. 1:20; Phil. 1:8; 1 Thess. 2:5,10). The issue is truthfulness, not restricting oaths.

entries.title: Matthew 5:34-36
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:34-36 This showed how elaborately the rabbis had developed" binding" and "unbinding" oaths (cf. Matt. 23:16-22). It was a way to appear to be telling the truth by associating one's statement with Deity, but all the time knowing that one's oath, expressed in certain ways, was not legally binding. Religious hypocrisy is always shocking!

entries.title: Matthew 5:37 "But let your statement be, 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:37 "But let your statement be, 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'" Jesus was concerned with truthfulness, not form (cf. James 5:12)! Others who claim to know God should be honest and trustworthy, not tricky.

Notice again how Jesus takes an OT quote and shows its appropriate understanding on a higher spiritual level.

▣
NASB  "evil"
NKJV, NRSV, REB, NET  "the evil one"
TEV, NJB  "the Evil One"
Peshitta  "a deception"

The inflected form of the term in Greek can either be NEUTER, "evil" or MASCULINE, "the evil one." This same ambiguity occurs in Matt. 6:13; 13:19,38; John. 17:15; 2 Thess. 3:3; 1 John. 2:13,14; 3:12; 5:18-19.

Evil has several forms.

  1. a fallen world system, Genesis 3; Eph. 2:2; James 4:4
  2. personal evil, Eph. 2:2
  3. fallen individuals, Eph. 2:3; James 4:1-2
  4. natural events (i.e storms, plagues, diseases, etc.)

Evil looks for an opportunity to kill, steal, and destroy. Only the mercy of God, His Son, and His Spirit can enable us to live happy, purposeful, contented lives in this fallen world (i.e. The Sermon On the Mount)!

Special Topic: Personal Evil

entries.title: Matthew 5:38 "an eye for an eye"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:38 "an eye for an eye" This is an allusion to Exod. 21:24, Lev. 24:20, and Deut. 19:21. This law, like divorce certificates, was originally intended to deal with a societal problem by attempting to limit personal revenge. It did not allow individuals or families to take unlimited revenge, but was a guideline for the court. It was often reduced to monetary equivalents by the Jewish judges. However, the principle of limited personal revenge remains.

Special Topic: Eye for Eye

entries.title: Matthew 5:39 "an evil person"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:39 "an evil person" This could, in context, refer to

  1. the first century legal system in the sense that it is better to endure additional insults than take a covenant brother to an unbelieving judge
  2. If "evil" relates to Matt. 5:37 and 1 Cor. 6, it could refer to the Evil One.
  3. The Charles B. Williams Translation, The New Testament in the Language of the People, gives a third option, "the one who injures you."
  4. For further thoughts on this subject, see Contextual Insights to 1 Corinthians 6.

entries.title: Matthew 5:39-42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:39-42 This was a series of five examples of Jesus' new ethics concerning our attitude toward others, both insiders and outsiders ( hyperboles). These are historically conditioned examples. They advocate an attitude, not a hard and fast rule for every society or age. It is the spirit of the believing offended party which should issue in positive actions of love. This should not be interpreted as covering inappropriate or repeated requests from tricky or lazy people.

entries.title: Matthew 5:40 "shirt. . .coat"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:40 "shirt. . .coat" The first item of clothing refers to an under garment and the second to an outer garment. This is a hyperbolic statement. Jesus is not advocating nudity! This is an allusion to Exod. 22:26-27; Deut. 24:10-13. The central truth of this entire section is that Christians should go beyond what others expect of them. The purpose is to encourage unbelievers to be attracted to God by His people's actions (cf. Matt. 5:16; 1 Pet. 2:12).

entries.title: Matthew 5:41
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:41 This is historically conditioned to a time when one nation militarily occupied another. The word "force" was of Persian derivation, originally referring to a postal carrier. It came to be the term used for forced labor of any kind by an occupying military or civil government. An example of this is Matt. 27:32. Christians are to go beyond even what is demanded or expected.

entries.title: Matthew 5:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:42 This was not meant to be taken as a hard and fast rule about lending, but an attitude of love and openness toward others, especially the poor, needy, and outcast (cf. Exod. 22:25; Deut. 15:7-11; Prov. 19:17).

The Sermon on the Mount is meant to illustrate Jesus as the "new Moses," but it should not be turned into a new Christian legalism! Jesus is exposing human sin by elevating the standard to a level no fallen human can obtain! The ethics of the New Covenant are only possible in a new mind, a new heart, and a new spirit (i.e. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). Even then, the fall of mankind in Gen. 3 still affects the believer!

Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind

entries.title: Matthew 5:43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:43 The quote referred to by Jesus is a composite.

  1. "You shall love your neighbor" is from Lev. 19:18.
    1. Jesus seems to see this as a crucial text, even listed with the Ten Commandments in Matt. 19:18-19.
    2. In Mark 12:31, it is the second greatest commandment after Deut. 6:4-5.
    3. In a similar way in Luke 10:25-28.
    4. Paul uses this text as a summary of the entire Law in Rom. 13:8-10.
  2. "And hate your enemy" is not a quote from the OT, but a commonly drawn inference by Jewish, exclusivistic religionists (i.e. Sadducees, Pharisee, Essenes).

How different is the new Kingdom ethic from the fallen world model of "self," "more for me at any cost," "what's in it for me"! Knowing God changes everything (cf. Matt. 5:20,48)!

entries.title: Matthew 5:44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:44 The KJV adds several phrases from Luke 6:27-28. They do not appear in ancient Greek uncial manuscripts א or B or several other geographically separated early manuscripts. The UBS4 gives the shorter reading an "A" rating (certain).

In this verse there are two PRESENT IMPERATIVES: "keep on loving and praying" and one PRESENT PARTICIPLE, "the one who keeps on persecuting." These PRESENTS speak of ongoing commands both of loving and forgiving on the part of the believer as well as the possibility of ongoing persecution.

The New Covenant is radically different from the current world order!

Special Topic: Textual Criticism

entries.title: Matthew 5:45 "that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:45 "that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven" Believers' lifestyles clearly reveal whose family they belong to: God's or Satan's. Children act like their fathers (cf. Lev. 19:2). If God cares and provides for "good" and "evil" people, so much more His people!

Special Topic: Sons of. . .(OT)

Special Topic: The Heavens and the Third Heaven

▣ Verse 45 clearly reveals God (Elohim of Gen. 1) as the Creator, Provider, and Sustainer of all life on the planet (i.e. Ps. 104:24-30; 145:14-16; Matt. 6:25-30; Acts 14:17).

  1. plant life
  2. animal life
  3. human life, both the good and evil

Special Topic: Names for Deity, C.

entries.title: Matthew 5:46 "rewards"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:46 "rewards" This was a recurrent theme in the Sermon on the Mount (cf. Matt. 6:1,2,4,6).

Special Topic: Degrees of Rewards and Punishment

5:48
NASB  "you are to be perfect"
NKJV  "you shall be perfect"
NRSV, Peshitta, NET  "be perfect"
TEV, NJB  "you must be perfect"
REB  "there must be no limit to your goodness"

This is an allusion to Lev. 11:44,45; 19:2; 20:7,26. This Hebrew term literally meant "that which is set apart" (BDB 871-2). The Greek term meant "complete," "mature," or "fully equiped for the assigned, divine task." This is a strong statement that God's ultimate standard of righteousness is Himself (cf. Deut. 18:13; see Special Topic: Righteousness). Humans cannot achieve perfection except in Christ (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21). However, believers must strive for it in their daily lives. There must be a theological balance between

  1. salvation being accepted as a free gift of God through Christ, which is called positional sanctification
  2. striving toward Christlikeness, which is called progressive sanctification

Some interpreters see this verse as a summary of the immediate paragraph only. If so, it would focus on the inclusive love of God that His children should emulate. For a good brief discussion on this issue, see Millard J. Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd ed., "Holiness," pp. 311-313.

Special Topic: Holy

Special Topic: NT Holiness/Sanctification

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.


  1. Did Jesus reinterpret the OT or change it?
  2. What does "fulfill" mean in Matt. 5:17 and 18?
  3. Can one lose his salvation for calling another person a derogatory name (Matt. 5:22)?
  4. What does Matt. 5:23-24 say to our modern worship practices?
  5. Is remarriage adultery?
  6. Is swearing in court a sin?
  7. Explain how Matt. 5:17-20 and 48 frame the rest of the verses.

entries.title: Matthew 5:46-47
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:46-47 The actions of believers must go beyond the expected social acts of unbelievers. These verses contain two THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCES which implied probable future action.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
